comments.text:
Um, I've noticed over my excess of years that almost anybody can look at a scene and appreciate the details of the scene that are important without much effort. The house is over there. The horse if in the middle;, There is a fenced in exercise arena behind and to the right of the horse. The horse has a halter. A human is holding the halter. The human may even know the name of the human. Now turn that around. It is very difficult and requires experience and training to go the other way and make a scene that is truly representative, at some level, of the original scene. The original mega-pixel scene is not resident in memory. The optical nervous system as broken it down into very large tokens, house, horse, human, exercise yard, and so forth. It codes them with colors. Animate it and a token representing the scene has some distortions applied to it that move the horse as if it is skittish with the human calming it and controlling it. The preprocessing of the video system needs to be broken down and analyzed. This should be fed to the AI. The AI should be taught to "paint" the scene, fixing dabs of paint until the scene, when reprocessed through the visual apparatus, looks correct. But, nowhere except at the first bits of video processing in the eye do the full gigapixels per sixtieth of a second of data exist. Each token has a highly variable stock of data to it with encoding that the baby human learns to apply to what reaches its eyes.

The same applies to the ears, smell, taste, proprioception, and so forth. Depending on what the human needs to be doing at a given time most of these heavily loaded tokens are ignored. And somehow we arrive at useful results. The LLM level in humans must be hidden behind very fancy tokenizing hardware that somehow discards what is not important at the time as it distills what is going on around it. Surely breathing is an important set of tokens. But they're handled well before the conscious part of the mind gets involve, most of the time. Tokenizing must somehow get feedback at all levels about what sort of tokens are interesting or not. LLMs are fancy memories. The ream juju must be in the tokenization. If the brain can handle say 4 chunks of data at a time make the chunks bigger and more loaded with meaning.

At least that is what my autistic half a mind sees when I get introspective enough. (And don't forget the gorilla in the background effect.)

comments.text: The missing world model is made really evident by some of the failures on the ARC-AGI benchmark, specifically the ones about colored areas made of blocks. We get it intuitively because we "see" how one color stretches out over another for example, but how could a model that operates on a raw sequence of input blocks figure it out? The problem is given as a sequence of colors going over the entire display panel like: "blue, red, blue, white, white…". A model would need to re-arrange these blocks and then analyze the image they produce. Then they can process images, but have no innate understanding of the concept of "this bit is stretching out and going over this block", as it is mostly our internal representation of physical concepts we're familiar with, having seen them from childhood and experienced them thousands of times. None of this is related to language or words or their representation as tokens, those are completely the wrong way to encode this sort of visual information. Models will not ace ARC-AGI until they go through this fundamental change and adopt a powerful world model.

comments.author: @CharlesVanNoland
comments.text: Anything that involves incrementally training on static "datasets" was always going to be a dead end. A proper general intelligence learns in real-time, directly from experience. You'll never achieve that with something that can only be incrementally 'trained' offline. You'll never achieve something that can walk/run/climb or articulate itself as proficiently as something that learned from experience how to do those things with something that learns offline and is incapable of learning from moment to moment. You definitely won't be changing the world either if your solution requires huge amounts of off-site compute. Compute needs to be self-contained. None of this is going to be feasible with backprop-trained network models or any kind of incremental gradient descent approach. What we need is a novel lightweight real-time learning algorithm that builds knowledge structures on-the-fly, and learns to abstract and solve problems as it gains experience, constructing spatiotemporal patterns of spatiotemporal patterns. Algorithms like Sparse Predictive Hierarchies, SoftHebb, Hierarchical Temporal Memory, etc... are more in the direction of what general intelligence will be like than anything involving offline "training". That's not to say that a static offline trained network can't play a role, it's just not going to be the end-all be-all to making a computer learn and think. The reality is that it's only people who can think outside of the offline backprop-trained network model who will end up being responsible for creating such things.
